strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP question: whether demographic persona prompting meaningfully diversifies LLM responses to moral and value questionnaires.

Seven models, two questionnaires, and repeated 200-persona samples provide useful empirical breadth. The item-level distributions support a descriptive finding of concentrated responses, particularly endorsement of harm avoidance and fairness, under the tested prompts.

The appendices provide prompt templates, questionnaire items, model identifiers, access dates, and persona-generation seeds. The authors also attempt manual validation of response parsing and acknowledge limitations of demographic sampling and questionnaire-based evaluation.
weaknesses: The central inference from aggregate stability to persona resistance is not established. Samples from the same persona distribution can produce nearly identical averages and correlations even when demographic subgroups differ substantially. Sections 3.1–3.2 need persona-conditioned effect estimates with uncertainty. Similarly, Section 3.4 does not define its variance estimator sufficiently or distinguish ordinary convergence of aggregate estimates from reduced variability in individual responses.

Essential comparisons are missing. The no-persona baseline announced in Section 2.2 is not quantitatively compared with persona-conditioned responses. Repeated responses to fixed personas and controlled changes between personas would help separate decoding variability from persona effects. Demographic diversity alone does not establish that the sampled personas should disagree about harm or fairness, so consensus does not necessarily indicate failed role adoption.

Questionnaire administration and scoring are insufficiently specified. Table 2 gives MFQ items PVQ-style similarity anchors, whereas Appendix B uses relevance anchors. Appendix E does not clearly specify respondent-level MRAT centering or explain the mapping from PVQ-RR’s 19 refined values to the ten reported dimensions. These could be reporting errors, but the implemented scales, item groupings, and scoring equations must be clarified before the value profiles can be confidently interpreted.

The response-parsing validation does not adequately cover the experimental setting. Human checking covers 89 unprompted Claude Haiku responses, with approximately 95% accuracy on PVQ-RR, rather than persona-conditioned outputs across all seven models. The larger parser comparison lacks a clearly reported human-reference evaluation. Refusals, ambiguous answers, and failed parses need explicit handling and coverage statistics; several bars in Figures 10–11 contain fewer than the stated 200 responses.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful model and prompt documentation. The WVS-derived sampling probabilities, generated persona sets, parser prompt, explicit decoding settings, and executable scoring procedure are not supplied. No code or response-data release is identified. Table 5 also omits Claude Opus’s third MFQ run despite Table 3 describing correlations across three runs.

Claims about fixed internal value orientations and the effects of alignment exceed the evidence from one demographic prompting template applied to aligned models. Training-data and RLHF explanations remain hypotheses without isolating comparisons. The descriptive observations are worth pursuing, but the inference and measurement gaps require substantive, feasible revisions before a sound Findings recommendation.
